experiments.name: BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids)
experiments.description: BASS investigated the burning and extinction characteristics of a wide variety of fuel samples in microgravity to guide material selection and fire safety strategies for spacecraft. The experiment tested thin and thick solid fuels in varying atmospheric conditions aboard the International Space Station, providing foundational data on how fire behaves differently without buoyancy-driven convection.
objectives: Determine flame spread rates over thin solid fuels in microgravity
Assess flammability limits of spacecraft-relevant materials in reduced gravity
Compare concurrent and opposed-flow flame spread in microgravity vs normal gravity
Evaluate the influence of oxygen concentration and flow velocity on flame behavior
Provide data to improve NASA-STD-6001 material flammability testing standards
key_findings: Concurrent flame spread rates over thin solid fuels in microgravity are 30-60% lower than in normal gravity at comparable conditions
Flame extinction occurs at lower oxygen concentrations in microgravity for some materials due to reduced buoyant flow and radiative heat losses
Thin fuels exhibit hemispherical blue flame structures in quiescent microgravity, contrasting with elongated yellow flames in 1g
Flow velocity has a non-monotonic effect on flame spread: low flows can extinguish flames by insufficient oxygen delivery, while very high flows can blow flames off
PMMA samples showed a critical flow velocity below which flames could not sustain in microgravity
safety_implications: Ground-based Test 1 flammability screening may not capture worst-case scenarios for some materials in microgravity
Material flammability rankings can change between 1g and microgravity conditions
Ventilation system design significantly affects fire propagation potential in spacecraft
Thin materials such as paper and fabric may be more hazardous than thick materials in microgravity under certain flow conditions

flame_characteristics.shape: Hemispherical to elongated depending on flow
flame_characteristics.color: Blue with yellow edges at higher oxygen concentrations

experiments.name: BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids - II)
experiments.description: BASS-II continued and expanded upon the original BASS experiment aboard the ISS. It investigated flame spread over flat composite and fabric samples in a flow duct, focusing on materials relevant to the Constellation program and future exploration vehicles. BASS-II also explored the effect of sample width and thickness on flame behavior in microgravity.
objectives: Extend flame spread measurements to wider and thicker fuel samples
Investigate the effect of sample geometry on flame behavior in microgravity
Test composite and multi-layer fabric materials used in advanced spacecraft designs
Determine conditions for flame growth versus extinction in realistic cabin airflow
Refine flammability screening criteria for exploration-class missions
key_findings: Wider samples exhibited edge effects that accelerated flame spread compared to narrow samples
Multi-layer fabrics showed complex burning behaviors with inter-layer flame spread
Thick PMMA samples showed a longer transient flame development phase in microgravity
Sample width-to-thickness ratio is a critical parameter for material flammability assessment
Flame spread showed greater sensitivity to oxygen concentration at low flow velocities
safety_implications: Standard small-scale flammability tests may underestimate fire risk for large material surfaces
Layered fabric assemblies require special consideration in spacecraft fire safety assessment
Material geometry and mounting configuration affect flammability behavior significantly

flame_characteristics.shape: Flat front spreading along surface with edge curling
flame_characteristics.color: Blue base with yellow-orange trailing flame

experiments.name: ACME-BRE (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator)
experiments.description: The Burning Rate Emulator used a gas burner to emulate the burning rates of solid and liquid fuels in a precisely controlled manner. By controlling fuel delivery rates to match real material pyrolysis, BRE enabled systematic study of how burning rate affects flame stability, extinction, and heat flux in microgravity without the complexity of solid fuel regression.
objectives: Emulate burning behavior of real materials using precisely controlled gas burners
Map flame stability and extinction limits as a function of burning rate and oxygen
Determine radiative and convective heat flux partitioning in microgravity flames
Validate computational models of solid fuel combustion using simplified gas-fed flames
Characterize the transition between stable and unstable burning regimes
materials_tested: Methane-nitrogen gas mixtures (emulating various solid fuel pyrolysis rates)
key_findings: Radiative heat loss is the dominant flame extinction mechanism in microgravity for large diffusion flames
A minimum burning rate exists below which flames cannot sustain in microgravity, analogous to the extinction limit of solid fuels
Increasing oxygen concentration shifts the burning rate stability map, broadening the range of sustainable flames
The emulator successfully reproduced flame stand-off distances observed in real solid fuel experiments
Near-extinction flames exhibit oscillatory behavior with periodic brightening and dimming
safety_implications: Quantified relationship between burning rate and fire sustainability aids in fire risk modeling
Data supports development of computational tools for spacecraft fire safety assessment
Understanding extinction limits helps define safe operating envelopes for cabin atmospheres

flame_characteristics.shape: Spherical to hemispherical on flat burner surface
flame_characteristics.color: Blue for lean mixtures, yellow-orange for sooty fuels

experiments.name: ACME-CLD (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame)
experiments.description: The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame experiment studied the structure, soot formation, and radiative emission of axisymmetric gaseous diffusion flames in microgravity. By eliminating buoyancy, CLD produced perfectly symmetric laminar diffusion flames that enabled precise comparison with computational flame models and advanced soot formation theories.
objectives: Create benchmark-quality laminar diffusion flame data for computational model validation
Measure soot volume fraction distributions in buoyancy-free diffusion flames
Quantify radiative heat flux and its role in microgravity flame structure
Determine smoke point (soot inception limit) for various fuel compositions in microgravity
Compare flame shapes and lengths between microgravity and normal gravity
key_findings: Microgravity diffusion flames are wider and shorter than their 1g counterparts due to the absence of buoyancy-induced flow acceleration
Soot formation in microgravity is enhanced compared to 1g for the same fuel flow conditions, leading to lower smoke points
Radiative losses from soot in microgravity flames are significantly higher due to longer soot residence times
Flame luminosity increases in microgravity due to higher soot volume fractions
Computational models using detailed soot kinetics agree well with microgravity flame data
safety_implications: Increased soot production in microgravity fires means more particulate smoke, requiring sensitive smoke detectors
Radiation-driven flame spread may be more significant in microgravity than in 1g
Smoke toxicity hazard is potentially greater in microgravity due to enhanced soot formation

flame_characteristics.color: Yellow-orange with luminous soot, blue base

experiments.name: ACME-SoFIE (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction)
experiments.description: ACME-SoFIE, part of the broader SoFIE program, studied the fundamental ignition and extinction processes of solid fuels in microgravity. It focused on determining the boundary between flammable and non-flammable conditions for materials used in spacecraft, supporting the development of NASA's next-generation material flammability screening methods.
objectives: Determine the flammability boundaries (ignition and extinction limits) for solid fuels in microgravity
Measure the minimum oxygen concentration and flow velocity required for ignition
Investigate the effect of external radiant heat flux on ignition delay and flame establishment
Quantify the critical conditions for flame extinction including oxygen, flow, and heat loss
Support development of a material flammability index for spacecraft design
materials_tested: PMMA flat samples of varying thickness
key_findings: Ignition delay times increase by 20-50% in microgravity compared to 1g for comparable heat fluxes
The minimum oxygen concentration for sustained burning of PMMA in microgravity is approximately 15-16%
External radiant heat flux is the dominant factor in determining ignition time, overriding flow velocity effects
A flammability map in oxygen-flow velocity space shows a well-defined flammable envelope for each material
Material thickness significantly affects the extinction boundary due to in-depth heat conduction losses
safety_implications: Ignition thresholds developed in 1g may not be conservative for all microgravity scenarios
Material thickness should be considered in flammability assessment, not just surface properties
The flammability envelope concept provides a practical tool for spacecraft material selection

flame_characteristics.shape: Hemispherical during ignition, transitioning to spreading front
flame_characteristics.color: Blue initially, developing yellow edges as flame grows

experiments.name: SAFFIRE-I (Spacecraft Fire Experiment I)
experiments.description: SAFFIRE-I was the first large-scale fire experiment conducted in space. Performed aboard the Northrop Grumman Cygnus resupply vehicle after it departed the ISS, SAFFIRE-I ignited a 0.4m × 0.95m sample of cotton-fiberglass blend fabric to study flame growth and spread at scales relevant to actual spacecraft fires. It provided unprecedented data on large fire behavior in microgravity.
objectives: Conduct the first large-scale fire growth experiment in microgravity
Determine if a large flame can sustain and spread over a realistic-sized material sample
Measure flame spread rate, heat release rate, and thermal environment of a large microgravity fire
Evaluate sensor performance for fire detection in spacecraft
Validate computational fire growth models at spacecraft-relevant scales
materials_tested: Cotton-fiberglass blend fabric (Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-speed, SIBAL)
key_findings: Large-scale flame spread was successfully sustained in microgravity for the first time
The flame spread rate over the large sample was approximately 1.0 cm/s, lower than small-scale ISS experiments at comparable conditions
Flame front was remarkably flat and uniform across the 40 cm sample width
Peak heat flux to the surrounding structure reached levels that could damage nearby equipment
Post-fire analysis showed complete combustion of the fabric with minimal residue
safety_implications: Confirmed that large fires can sustain and grow in microgravity spacecraft environments
Heat flux measurements inform structural fire protection design requirements
Fire detection sensors must be calibrated for the different smoke signatures of microgravity fires
Validated that fire modeling tools can be extended to spacecraft-scale scenarios

flame_characteristics.shape: Flat uniform front across full sample width
flame_characteristics.color: Orange-yellow luminous flame with blue leading edge

experiments.name: SAFFIRE-II (Spacecraft Fire Experiment II)
experiments.description: SAFFIRE-II focused on the material flammability screening aspect, testing nine small samples of different materials in the Cygnus vehicle. Unlike SAFFIRE-I's large single sample, SAFFIRE-II evaluated multiple materials simultaneously, assessing their relative flammability in a realistic spacecraft atmosphere and airflow.
objectives: Evaluate the flammability of multiple spacecraft-relevant materials in microgravity
Compare material flammability rankings between microgravity and standard 1g testing (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1)
Assess the accuracy of ground-based screening tests for microgravity fire prediction
Measure flame spread rates and thermal signatures for each material sample
Determine if any materials that pass ground-based testing fail in actual microgravity
key_findings: Material flammability rankings in microgravity showed several differences compared to 1g Test 1 results
Some materials that barely passed ground-based flammability tests sustained flames in microgravity at comparable conditions
Silicone rubber showed higher than expected flammability in microgravity due to reduced dripping and falling of melted material
Teflon and Kapton remained flame-resistant in microgravity, consistent with ground-based testing
Nomex showed borderline flammability behavior, with flames that self-extinguished after brief propagation
safety_implications: Ground-based Test 1 results do not always predict microgravity flammability accurately
Material selection for spacecraft should include supplemental microgravity flammability data
Some borderline materials require re-evaluation for use in exploration vehicles
Self-extinguishing behavior observed in 1g may not occur in microgravity for certain materials

flame_characteristics.shape: Varies by material — flat fronts on fabrics, receding spherical on polymers

experiments.name: SAFFIRE-III (Spacecraft Fire Experiment III)
experiments.description: SAFFIRE-III repeated the large-scale fire experiment of SAFFIRE-I with a thicker composite material sample and higher airflow velocity. It aimed to determine the effect of material thickness and increased ventilation on large fire behavior in microgravity, simulating a more challenging fire scenario.
objectives: Investigate large-scale fire growth with thicker fuel samples in microgravity
Assess the effect of higher forced airflow on large flame behavior
Determine if increased airflow accelerates or suppresses large fires in microgravity
Measure heat release rate and total heat output for thicker burning materials
Provide additional data points for computational fire growth model validation
materials_tested: Cotton-fiberglass blend fabric (SIBAL) — thicker composite layup
key_findings: Flame spread rate increased with higher airflow velocity, contrary to some small-scale predictions
Thicker samples burned for a longer duration with higher total heat release
The flame front remained relatively uniform but showed more instability at higher flows
Peak structural temperatures exceeded those measured in SAFFIRE-I
Post-combustion residue analysis showed incomplete combustion at the thicker sample core
safety_implications: Higher ventilation rates can exacerbate fire growth for large fires in microgravity
Thicker materials pose a greater thermal hazard due to prolonged burning and higher heat release
Ventilation system shutdown is critical for fire suppression in spacecraft
Fire protection design must account for worst-case ventilation scenarios

flame_characteristics.shape: Broad flat front with undulating edges at high flow

experiments.name: FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment)
experiments.description: FLEX studied the burning and extinction of isolated fuel droplets in microgravity. The experiment revealed the extraordinary phenomenon of 'cool flame' burning — a low-temperature combustion mode that persists after visible flame extinction. FLEX provided fundamental insights into droplet combustion dynamics and the previously unknown cool flame regime.
objectives: Measure burning rates and extinction diameters of isolated fuel droplets in microgravity
Determine the effect of fuel composition and ambient oxygen on droplet flame extinction
Discover and characterize non-visible low-temperature combustion modes (cool flames)
Validate droplet combustion theory and computational models in buoyancy-free conditions
Investigate the role of radiative heat loss in droplet flame extinction
key_findings: Discovered 'cool flame' combustion: after visible flame extinction, droplets continued to burn in a low-temperature, non-luminous mode
Cool flames are sustained by low-temperature oxidation chemistry (below ~700K) and can persist for extended periods
Droplet burning rates in microgravity agree well with classical d-squared law during the quasi-steady phase
Radiative heat loss is the primary cause of hot-flame extinction in large droplets
Extinction diameter scales with initial droplet diameter and ambient oxygen concentration
Cool flame burning produces different combustion products, including aldehydes and peroxides
safety_implications: Cool flames represent an invisible fire hazard that conventional optical detectors cannot see
Low-temperature combustion products (aldehydes, peroxides) are toxic and require chemical sensing
Fuel spills in microgravity could sustain non-visible burning for extended periods
Fire suppression systems must account for re-ignition from cool flame regions

flame_characteristics.shape: Spherical envelope surrounding droplet (hot flame); invisible shell (cool flame)

experiments.name: FLEX-2 (Flame Extinguishment Experiment 2)
experiments.description: FLEX-2 continued the droplet combustion research of FLEX with a focus on multi-component fuels, larger droplet sizes, and the systematic characterization of cool flame dynamics. The experiment mapped the conditions under which cool flames arise and determined the chemical pathways responsible for this unusual combustion mode.
objectives: Characterize cool flame dynamics as a function of fuel type, droplet size, and ambient conditions
Investigate multi-component fuel droplet burning and its relevance to practical liquid fuel spills
Measure the chemical products of cool flame combustion for toxicity assessment
Determine if cool flames can transition back to hot flame ignition under certain conditions
Provide comprehensive dataset for development of cool flame chemical kinetic models
key_findings: Cool flames can persist for up to 20 seconds after hot flame extinction for large droplets
Cool flame burning rate is approximately 50-70% lower than hot flame burning rate
Bi-component droplets showed preferential vaporization effects that delayed cool flame onset
Elevated pressure significantly extends the cool flame duration and broadens the cool flame regime
Cool-to-hot flame re-ignition was observed under specific conditions of higher pressure and oxygen
Gas chromatography analysis confirmed formaldehyde and hydrogen peroxide as primary cool flame products
safety_implications: Extended cool flame duration increases window of invisible fire hazard
Multi-component fuel spills may behave unpredictably with different cool flame characteristics
Cool-to-hot flame re-ignition possibility means suppressed fires could reignite spontaneously
Cabin atmosphere monitoring must include chemical sensors for aldehyde detection

flame_characteristics.shape: Spherical (hot flame); diffuse spherical shell (cool flame)

experiments.name: SPICE (Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment)
experiments.description: SPICE measured the smoke point — the critical condition at which soot begins to escape from a laminar diffusion flame — for various gaseous fuels in microgravity. Understanding soot emission limits is crucial for predicting smoke generation from fires in spacecraft and designing effective smoke detection systems.
objectives: Determine the smoke point for multiple fuel types in microgravity coflow diffusion flames
Compare microgravity smoke points with 1g measurements to assess buoyancy effects
Quantify the relationship between fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, and soot emission onset
Evaluate the effect of inert dilution of fuel on smoke point behavior
Provide data for improving computational soot models
key_findings: Smoke points in microgravity are consistently lower than in 1g, meaning soot emission occurs at lower fuel flow rates
The reduction in smoke point from 1g to microgravity ranges from 30-50% depending on fuel type
Longer soot residence times in microgravity flames allow more soot growth and aggregation
Coflow velocity has a significant effect on smoke point, with higher coflow delaying soot emission
Nitrogen dilution of fuel increases the smoke point proportionally in both 1g and microgravity
safety_implications: Fires in microgravity produce more smoke per unit fuel consumed than equivalent 1g fires
Smoke detectors for spacecraft must have higher sensitivity than ground-based systems
Ventilation airflow affects smoke dispersion patterns, influencing detector placement
Smoke toxicity assessment should account for microgravity-specific soot characteristics

flame_characteristics.shape: Elongated conical with rounded tip at smoke point transition
flame_characteristics.color: Blue base transitioning to yellow-orange tip; bright orange soot wings at smoke point

experiments.name: SoFIE (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction)
experiments.description: SoFIE is NASA's flagship ongoing microgravity combustion research facility aboard the ISS. It investigates the conditions under which solid materials ignite, burn, and extinguish in microgravity to support fire safety for Artemis lunar missions and future Mars transit vehicles. SoFIE encompasses multiple sub-experiments studying diverse materials under conditions representative of exploration atmospheres.
objectives: Map the complete flammability boundaries for spacecraft materials in exploration atmospheres
Investigate burning behavior at reduced pressures (8.2 psia / 56.5 kPa) with enriched oxygen (34%)
Determine ignition and extinction limits as a function of oxygen, pressure, and flow
Support development of NASA's next-generation material flammability screening standard
Test materials planned for use in Artemis lunar surface habitats and transit vehicles
Study flame spread, regression, and thermal hazard for thick solid fuels
key_findings: Exploration atmosphere (34% O2, 56.5 kPa) shows increased flammability for most materials compared to standard ISS atmosphere
PMMA flammability boundary shifts to lower flow velocities in reduced pressure exploration atmosphere
Material rankings for flammability change between standard and exploration atmospheres
Radiative ignition thresholds are lower in exploration atmosphere due to enhanced oxygen availability
Thin PMMA samples in exploration atmosphere show flame spread rates comparable to standard atmosphere at 1g
safety_implications: Exploration atmosphere conditions may require more stringent material selection criteria
Material flammability databases must be expanded to include exploration-relevant atmospheric conditions
Fire detection and suppression systems must be designed for the specific atmospheric conditions of each vehicle
Habitat design for lunar and Martian missions requires new fire safety protocols based on SoFIE results

flame_characteristics.color: Blue to blue-white at low O2, brighter yellow at 34% O2
